title: Which digits hide behind BYE × 6 = RAY?
description: A three digit number with letters B Y E is multiplied by six to give R A Y. The video fixes B from the size, lists the even choices for Y, and tests each choice against the rule that different letters hide different digits. Keeko doubts the list of choices for Y and wants to include eight.
teaching_notes: One idea: fix the first digit from the size, list what the last digit can be, then test each case for a clash. Watch for students who list every even digit for Y without checking that the answer stays three digits.

video_script.why: The child has solved letter puzzles with addition, and now meets one with multiplication.
video_script.substitution: Fix B from the size, list the even choices for Y, and test each case for clashing digits.
video_script.anchor: the letter puzzle BYE × 6 = RAY of the book, reasoned out by {{NAME_1}}
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says Y is even, so Y can be 8 as well. But 180 × 6 = 1080 has four digits, and RAY has three.
video_script.payoff_line: One hundred and five times six is six hundred and thirty.

final_answer.spoken: one hundred and five times six is six hundred and thirty

names.{{NAME_1}}: the child who reasons about BYE x 6 = RAY

maths_rules: BYE × 6 = RAY, five different letters B, Y, E, R, A, and B, R are not 0
6 × E is even, so its last digit Y is even; Y cannot be 7 or more because 170 × 6 = 1020 has four digits; so Y is 0, 2, 4 or 6
180 × 6 = 1080 has four digits, so Y is not 8
Y = 2: 6 × E ends in 2 for E = 2 or 7; E = 2 repeats Y; 127 × 6 = 762 gives R = 7 = E, so it fails
Y = 4: 6 × E ends in 4 for E = 4 or 9; E = 4 repeats Y; 149 × 6 = 894 gives A = 9 = E, so it fails
Y = 6: 6 × E ends in 6 for E = 1 or 6; E = 1 repeats B and E = 6 repeats Y, so it fails
Y = 0: 6 × E ends in 0 for E = 0 or 5; E = 0 repeats Y; 105 × 6 = 630 gives R = 6, A = 3, Y = 0, and 1, 0, 5, 6, 3 are all different
video_script.design: One puzzle BYE × 6 = RAY. B is fixed by size, Y is listed by evenness and size, and the four cases of Y are tested one by one.

<bookmark mark='one'/>A bigger B is worse, and B is not zero, so B is one.

<bookmark mark='big'/>One hundred and seventy times six is one thousand and twenty, which is too big.
<bookmark mark='list'/>Y can only be zero, two, four or six.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks Y can be eight, because eight is even too.
<bookmark mark='test'/>But one hundred and eighty times six is one thousand and eighty, which has four digits.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Evenness is not enough. The size of the answer must also stay at three digits.
